headline: The pope chose a care home first. Then 2.5 million at Mass.
summary: Pope Leo XIV began his first full day in Argentina on Monday at the Cottolengo Don Orione, a home south of Buenos Aires for more than 400 people with disabilities. He told them their lives are a blessing, not a burden. President Javier Milei's cuts froze payments to homes like it. Then he said Mass for a crowd AP News put at 2.5 million.

cover_question.q: Why did the pope go there first?

cover_answer: To make a point. The government cut money to homes like it.
table_question: If you lose a vote at home, do you still have to go along with it?

5-7.script: The pope is visiting Argentina, a country at the bottom of South America. On Monday he went first to a home where 400 people with disabilities live, about as many as a whole school. He hugged people in wheelchairs and told them their lives are a blessing. Some cried happy tears, then millions came to pray with him.
5-7.why: The hug and the crowd are the story here. The budget fight stays off the card.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and reads your face before your words, so the script gives them a hug, a home the size of a school and happy tears, and leaves the frozen payments out. Expect 'why do they live there?' Say some people need help every day, and that home is where they get it.

8-12.script: Argentina's president, Javier Milei, cut spending hard, and payments for people with disabilities froze. Congress passed a law to fund them over his veto; he still hasn't paid. On Monday the pope made a home for 400 of them his first stop. Like a referee pointing at a rule the players stopped following.
8-12.why: A law passed and not paid: a fairness chain they can follow.
8-12.why_long: Between eight and twelve a child is testing whether adults follow their own rules, so the script hands them a chain: a law passed over a veto, money still unpaid, a visitor pointing at it. The referee is the mechanism. Expect 'can he get in trouble for not paying?' Say the report doesn't say, and that the Senate votes on the money soon.

13-17.script: If a law passes over your veto, can you just not pay? Argentina's Congress voted more money for disability care over Milei's veto; his government hasn't paid, and the home the pope visited Monday is still owed. Second: he never named Milei. Does a rebuke count if you skip the name?
13-17.why: Two open questions. Let them argue the first before you add the second.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a leader who balanced the budget and a law he will not fund. The script asks them to weigh that before judging the pope for leaving Milei's name out. Expect 'so was the pope being political?' Say he quoted church teaching and let them decide where that line sits.

5-7.a: Happy tears, mostly. The pope came to their home and said they matter.

8-12.q: Why did the pope go there first?
8-12.a: To make a point. The home is still owed money the government froze.

8-12.q: Can the pope make Milei pay?
8-12.a: No. He has no power in Argentina. The Senate votes on the money soon.

13-17.q: Was the visit a political stunt?
13-17.a: He never named Milei, and the money the home is owed is real either way.

13-17.q: Does a visit like this change anything?
13-17.a: Unknown. Congress voted the money over his veto. He hasn't paid.
